tips.title: Potable is not pure
tips.body: **Potable** water is safe to drink: low enough in **dissolved salts** and **microbes**. It is **not pure** in the chemical sense, because it still contains dissolved substances. Writing that drinking water is pure water loses the mark every time.

tips.title: Choose, filter, sterilise
tips.body: For fresh water in the UK the three steps are: **choose** an appropriate source, pass it through **filter beds**, then **sterilise** it. Filtering removes solids you can see; sterilising kills the microbes you cannot.

tips.title: Three sterilising agents
tips.body: **Chlorine**, **ozone** or **ultraviolet light**. All three kill microbes; only the first is a chemical added to the water. If a question asks for a sterilising agent, any of the three earns the mark.

tips.title: Desalination costs energy
tips.body: Where fresh water is scarce, sea water is treated by **distillation** or by **reverse osmosis** through membranes. Both need **large amounts of energy**, which is why desalination is a last resort rather than a first choice.

tips.title: Sludge is anaerobic, effluent is aerobic
tips.body: In sewage treatment the **sludge** is digested **anaerobically** — without oxygen, producing methane — while the **effluent** gets **aerobic** biological treatment, with air bubbled through. Swapping the two is the commonest slip in this topic.

why.matters:
**Pure** and **safe to drink** are different requirements, and this topic is about the second one. Tap water is a mixture and always will be; what matters is that the dissolved salts are low enough and the microbes are gone.

So water treatment is a sequence of steps, each aimed at something specific: filter out what you can see, sterilise what you cannot. And where there is no fresh water to start from, the salt has to be taken out of sea water — which is chemistry you pay for in energy.

examples.title: Tap water is not pure, and should not be
examples.body:
A bottle labelled *pure spring water* is a mixture, and so is everything out of a tap. **Potable** means safe to drink: low enough in dissolved salts and free of microbes. It does not mean there is nothing in it.

Genuinely pure water is made in a lab, tastes flat, and is not what anybody wants in a kettle — the dissolved minerals are most of the taste. Getting this distinction right is worth a mark, and it is also why *pure* on a label is an advertising word rather than a chemical one.

visual.alt: A table setting pure water, which is a single substance with nothing dissolved in it, against potable water, which is safe to drink with low levels of dissolved salts and no microbes, and is what comes out of a tap

examples.title: Why desalination is a last resort
examples.body:
Taking the salt out of sea water is easy to describe and expensive to do. Distillation means **boiling the water away** and condensing it, and boiling is where the energy goes: heating a litre from room temperature to 100 °C takes **336 kJ**, and turning that same litre into steam takes **2260 kJ** more.

That is about 22 minutes of a two-kilowatt kettle **per litre**. Reverse osmosis pushes the water through a membrane instead and avoids the boiling, which is why it is the method that scaled — but it still needs pressure, and pressure still needs power.

props.caption: Distilling one litre. Almost all of it is the evaporation.

visual.alt: Two bars in proportion for distilling a litre of water: three hundred and thirty-six kilojoules to heat it to boiling against two thousand two hundred and sixty to turn it into steam, so almost all the energy is the evaporation

examples.title: Why a sewage works runs on its own gas
examples.body:
Sewage treatment splits into two halves that need opposite conditions, and it is worth knowing which is which.

The **sludge** that settles out is digested **anaerobically** — without oxygen — and the bacteria that do it give off **methane**, which many works burn to generate their own electricity. The **effluent** above it gets the opposite treatment: air bubbled through, so **aerobic** bacteria can break down what is left. Same plant, two populations of bacteria, kept deliberately apart.

visual.alt: A flow chart of sewage treatment: screening out solids, letting the sludge settle, then digesting the sludge without air to give methane while the effluent above it is treated with air bubbled through

steps.title: What potable water is
steps.body:
Water of appropriate quality is essential for life. Water that is **safe to drink** is called **potable water**.

To be potable, water must have **sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes**. It does not have to contain nothing at all.

**Potable water is not pure water.** In chemistry, a pure substance is a single substance with nothing else in it. Drinking water contains **dissolved substances** — calcium and magnesium salts, fluoride, small amounts of chlorine — so it is a **mixture**, not a pure substance. That distinction is examined regularly, and "tap water is pure" is simply wrong.

**The method used depends on what water is available**, and on local conditions.

**In the United Kingdom**, rain provides water with low levels of dissolved substances — **fresh water** — which collects in the ground, and in lakes and rivers. Most potable water here is produced by three steps:

1. **Choose an appropriate source of fresh water.**
2. **Pass the water through filter beds** — this removes insoluble solids, grit and larger particles.
3. **Sterilise it** — this kills microbes.

**Sterilising agents** used are **chlorine**, **ozone**, **ultraviolet light**.

visuals.alt: A flowchart of the three stages used to produce potable water from fresh water in the United Kingdom, ending in potable water

steps.title: When fresh water runs short
steps.body:
Not every country has the UK's rainfall. **If supplies of fresh water are limited**, potable water has to be made from **salty water or sea water**, by **desalination**.

There are two methods.

**Distillation.** The salt water is **boiled**, the steam is collected and **condensed**, and the dissolved salts are left behind because they do not evaporate. The distilled water is then treated as usual.

**Reverse osmosis.** The salt water is forced at high pressure through a **membrane** with pores small enough to let water molecules through but not the larger dissolved ions.

**Both require large amounts of energy** — boiling water needs a great deal of heat, and forcing it through a membrane needs high pressure. That energy is expensive and, if it comes from fossil fuels, damaging. It is why desalination is used only where there is no fresh water available.

**Comparing the sources.** The ease of producing potable water depends on what you start with:

- **Ground water** is easiest: it already has few dissolved solids, so filtering and sterilising is enough.
- **Waste water** is harder: organic matter and harmful microbes must be removed first.
- **Salty or sea water** is hardest: the dissolved salts must be removed, which needs a lot of energy.

steps.title: Treating waste water
steps.body:
Urban lifestyles and industrial processes produce **large amounts of waste water**, which must be treated before it is released into the environment.

**What has to come out depends on where it came from.**

- **Sewage** and **agricultural** waste water need **organic matter** and **harmful microbes** removed.
- **Industrial** waste water may need **organic matter** and **harmful chemicals** removed — the extra chemical load is what makes industrial effluent different.

**Sewage treatment has four stages, in order:**

1. **Screening and grit removal** — removing large solids and grit that would damage the machinery.
2. **Sedimentation, producing sewage sludge and effluent** — the solids settle out as **sludge**, leaving liquid **effluent** above.
3. **Anaerobic digestion of the sewage sludge** — bacteria break the sludge down **without oxygen**, producing methane that can be burned for energy, and a residue usable as fertiliser.
4. **Aerobic biological treatment of the effluent** — air is bubbled through so **aerobic** bacteria break down the remaining organic matter and microbes.

**The two biological stages differ.** The sludge is treated **anaerobically** (no oxygen); the effluent is treated **aerobically** (air bubbled through). Learn them as a pair, because questions ask which is which.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Keep potable and pure apart.** Potable means **safe to drink**, with low levels of dissolved salts and microbes. Pure means a **single substance**. Tap water is potable and impure at the same time, and saying so correctly is often worth a mark on its own.

**Name the sterilising agent.** "It is sterilised" is weaker than "sterilised using **chlorine**, **ozone** or **ultraviolet light**". Naming one costs nothing.

**Say what each stage removes.** Filter beds remove **insoluble solids**; sterilising kills **microbes**. A question asking why both are needed wants that contrast — neither step does the other's job.

**Get the two biological stages the right way round.** Sludge → **anaerobic**; effluent → **aerobic**. A useful hook: sludge is thick and airless, so the bacteria work without oxygen.

**Explain why desalination is a last resort.** Not merely "it is expensive" but *it needs large amounts of energy, which costs money and, if generated from fossil fuels, releases carbon dioxide*. That links the topic to sustainability, which is what the unit is about.

**Justify a ranking with what must be removed.** Ground water needs only filtering and sterilising; waste water also needs organic matter and microbes gone; sea water needs **dissolved salts** removed, which no filter can do. The order follows from the chemistry, not from opinion.

**In the practical, heat to constant mass.** Weigh, heat again, and reweigh until the mass stops changing — otherwise trapped water inflates the result. And **cool before weighing**, because a hot dish sets up convection currents that make the balance read low.

**Industrial waste water is the odd one out.** It may carry **harmful chemicals** as well as organic matter, so it needs treatment that sewage does not.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Potable water** is safe to drink: low levels of **dissolved salts** and **microbes**.
- It is **not pure** — it contains dissolved substances, so it is a mixture.
- UK fresh water: **choose an appropriate source of fresh water**, **pass the water through filter beds**, **sterilise it**.
- Filter beds remove **insoluble solids**; sterilising kills **microbes**.
- Sterilising agents: **chlorine**, **ozone**, **ultraviolet light**.
- Where fresh water is limited, **desalination** of salty or sea water by **distillation** or **reverse osmosis**.
- Both desalination methods need **large amounts of energy**.
- **Waste water** must be treated before release. Sewage and agricultural waste need **organic matter** and **microbes** removed; industrial waste may also need **harmful chemicals** removed.
- Sewage treatment: **screening and grit removal**; **sedimentation, producing sewage sludge and effluent**; **anaerobic digestion of the sewage sludge**; **aerobic biological treatment of the effluent**.
- **Sludge → anaerobic**, **effluent → aerobic**.
- Ease of producing potable water: **ground water**, then **waste water**, then **salty or sea water**.
- **Required practical 8**: analyse and purify water samples — pH, dissolved solids, distillation.
- Evaporate to find dissolved solids; **cool before weighing** and heat to **constant mass**.

questions.prompt: Explain why sewage sludge is treated anaerobically but effluent is treated aerobically.
questions.solution:
The **sludge** is thick and settles out, so oxygen cannot reach through it. **Anaerobic** bacteria digest it without oxygen, producing **methane** that can be burned for energy and a residue usable as fertiliser.

The **effluent** is a liquid through which **air can be bubbled**, so **aerobic** bacteria are used to break down the remaining organic matter and microbes. Aerobic treatment is faster, which suits the larger volume of liquid.

questions.prompt: Sea water contains about 35 g/dm³ of dissolved solids. What mass, in grams, would be left if 200 cm³ were evaporated to dryness?

A town on a dry coastline has no fresh water source but does have a sewage treatment works and access to the sea.

Compare producing potable water by treating waste water with producing it by desalinating sea water. Include the treatment each requires and the energy implications. (6 marks)
questions.solution:
**Treating waste water** means removing **organic matter** and **harmful microbes**. The sewage works already does most of this: screening and grit removal take out large solids, sedimentation separates **sludge** from **effluent**, the sludge is digested **anaerobically** and the effluent treated **aerobically**. To make the result potable it would then need filtering and **sterilising** with chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.

**Desalinating sea water** is a different problem. The salts are **dissolved**, so no filter can remove them; the water must be **distilled** — boiled and the steam condensed — or forced at high pressure through a membrane by **reverse osmosis**.

The decisive difference is **energy**. Boiling large volumes of water, or maintaining the pressure needed for reverse osmosis, requires **large amounts of energy**, which is expensive and, if generated from fossil fuels, releases carbon dioxide. Treating waste water uses far less, and the anaerobic digestion stage even **produces methane** that can be burned to offset some of the cost.

On energy and cost, treating the waste water is clearly preferable. Against that, the town would have to be confident that **harmful chemicals** from any industrial effluent had been removed, and public acceptance of recycled sewage can be a real obstacle. Given the energy figures, treating waste water is the better option provided the chemical monitoring is thorough.

examTechnique.body:
Potable water is **safe to drink**, not **pure** — it still contains dissolved substances. For UK fresh water the route is **choose the source, filter beds, sterilise**, with **chlorine, ozone or UV**.

Where fresh water is scarce, **desalination** by **distillation** or **reverse osmosis** removes dissolved salts but needs **large amounts of energy**. In sewage treatment, remember **sludge is anaerobic** and **effluent is aerobic**.

Weighing an evaporating dish while it is still hot.
Not heating to constant mass in the practical.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer distinguishes potable from pure and can say why tap water is both drinkable and a mixture. It names the sterilising agent rather than saying the water is cleaned, explains what each treatment stage removes and why neither filtering nor sterilising can substitute for the other, and gets the anaerobic and aerobic stages the right way round with a reason. It explains desalination's drawback as an energy demand with a carbon consequence, ranks water sources by what has to be removed, and in the practical cools the dish and heats to constant mass.
